strengths: Well-motivated problem: exploiting proprioception and multi-contact tactile feedback as explicit geometric constraints for 3D reconstruction under hand occlusion is a meaningful gap in the literature, which is dominated by vision-only occlusion-aware generation methods.

Technically sound and clearly described pipeline: pose-aware camera-aligned SDF representation, Structure-VAE with Eikonal/normal regularization, conditional flow-matching model with pretraining/finetuning stages, and physically motivated contact-consistency and non-interpenetration losses used both as training objectives and as decoder-guided sampling terms. The architecture and math are presented in good detail, aiding reproducibility.

Comprehensive experimental validation: results span simulation (with occlusion-stratified bins), real-world deployment on a humanoid robot with an unseen end-effector, and a DexYCB comparison against human-hand-specific baselines ([2],[39]) despite domain mismatch, showing competitive reconstruction rate and quality.

Thorough ablation study isolating sensing modalities (vision-only, no-touch), robustness to input noise (mask, kinematic, tactile), and model components (guidance, physics losses, contact representation type), which convincingly supports the individual contribution of each proposed component.
Cross-embodiment generalization is explicitly tested (training end-effectors differ from the real robot's), which is a valuable and non-trivial demonstration of practical applicability.
Honest discussion of limitations (calibration/pose sensitivity, fixed grid resolution, camera-aligned vs. object-centric frame) that appropriately contextualizes the claims rather than overselling.
weaknesses: The real-world experiment is limited in scale (5 objects, one embodiment, no dedicated ablation isolating vision vs. touch vs. proprioception contributions on real hardware), so the strength of the sim-to-real claim is somewhat constrained; the reported improvement over SAM3D in the real setting is marginal on several metrics (e.g., F@0.02 is worse than SAM3D).

Baselines (Amodal3R, SAM3D) are vision-only and not designed to leverage touch/proprioception, making the comparison somewhat unbalanced in favor of the proposed method; a more informative comparison might include a vision+depth or vision+proprioception baseline that does not use the same architecture family to strengthen the claim that gains come from physical grounding rather than architecture/training-data differences.

F@0.02 is not improved by the proposed method relative to SAM3D in the least-occluded bin and even in the aggregate 'All' row in Table 1 (SAM3D 0.228 vs Ours 0.189), which the paper acknowledges but does not deeply analyze; a clearer explanation of why fine-grained surface metrics sometimes favor the baseline would strengthen the paper.

Pose estimation comparison against SAM3D uses ground-truth depth for the baseline's best case, which is a somewhat favorable setup for the proposed method; a more apples-to-apples comparison (e.g., with realistic/noisy depth for SAM3D) would make the pose estimation gains more convincing.

The method depends heavily on accurate calibration (camera-hand extrinsics, forward kinematics) and a fixed 64^3 grid resolution shared between hand and object, which the authors note reduces effective object resolution in manipulation scenes; the practical impact of this on fine geometric detail (e.g., thin structures) is not quantitatively assessed beyond qualitative discussion.

Reproducibility relies on several closed or complex components (grasp-synthesis model [71], SLat pipeline adapted from [75], SAM3D refinement) and large-scale training data mixtures (3D-FUTURE, HSSD, ABO, ObjaverseXL subset, GSO) that are not all standard or trivially reproducible from the paper alone; code/data release is not explicitly promised in the manuscript excerpt provided.
